Like Freud, Carl Jung spent a great deal of time studying the�unconscious�mind. However, these great psychologists had differing views on the factors that determine human behavior. Freud narrowed it down to early childhood experiences. Jung emphasized that goals play an important role in directing human behavior.

Jung believed that the�unconscious�mind could be divided into two parts: the�personal unconscious�and the�collective�unconscious.


The�personal unconscious�comes from our own past experiences that we were once aware of, but have now been forgotten. Any basic habit you learned in early childhood has now become automatic for you to do and you don t have to consciously remember it step by step every time you do it.

For example, brushing your teeth, tying your shoes, raising your hand to ask or answer a question, and looking both ways before crossing the street come from your�personal unconscious.

The�collective�unconscious�is a powerful region of the mind and contains all the memories from our earliest ancestors. The�collective�unconscious�is the same for everyone around the world; it is universal. The�collective�unconscious�refers to human understandings common to all people because of our similar experiences. Any experience that might be experienced by everyone in the world can become part of the�collective�unconscious.

Examples of the�collective�unconscious�include: being wary of loud, thundering noises accompanying sudden flashes of intense light because that combination usually means personal danger (like lightning strikes, gas explosions, gunshots, and artillery fire); the physical sensations and emotional upheaval that accompany falling in love; and the need to explain the world around us.

It is interesting to note that many cultures around the world have similar myths, stories, and religious beliefs. This speaks to the�collective�unconscious. Every major religion and culture in recorded history has a description of the creation of the world and all the creatures in it, the reason existence of evil and pain in the world, a near-destruction of the world story (usually by flood), and a savior tale. Many of these explanations and descriptions of natural phenomena and religious beliefs are nearly identical even though the circumstances in which they developed are very far apart geographically, chronologically, and culturally.
